title: Harvard 31-7 New Hampshire (Sep 19, 2026) Game Recap - ESPN
content: DURHAM, N.C. -- — Nate Bailey scored two touchdowns in the final minute of the first half and Harvard capitalized on three takeaways to beat New Hampshire 31-7 on Saturday. Harvard, the three-time defending Ivy League champion, opened its season ranked No. 25 in the Stats Perform poll against fellow 2025 playoff participant New Hampshire. The Crimson pulled away late in the second quarter with 14 quick points. Bailey gave Harvard a 14-7 lead with 53 seconds left in the first half on a 23-yard reverse. Then DJ Thomas intercepted a pass along the sideline and returned it 30 yards, leading to Bailey’s 13-yard touchdown grab on the next play to make it 21-7 with 18 seconds left. Xaden Benson intercepted a deep pass in the endzone midway through the third quarter to keep Harvard’s two-touchdown lead. The Crimson settled for a short field goal following a 13-play drive and Xaviah Bascon scored on a 1-yard run with 8:48 left in the fourth. Charlie Smith threw for 71 yards and a touchdown for Harvard (1-0). Bascon finished with 51 yards rushing. Brooks Bentley was intercepted two times for New Hampshire (1-3). He finished 18 of 37 for 186 yards and added a 1-yard touchdown run. New Hampshire: At Sacred Heart next Saturday. title: Dear UNH community, stop using AI slop for graphics - The Charger Bulletin
content: Students, professors, faculty, organizations and everyone else? Stop using AI slop for your graphics. I don’t want to see these flyers, advertisements, social media posts and logos that have zero soul, dedication or creativity. They are all ugly and all come across as lazy and unengaging. Over the past few years, Gen Z has gotten more concerned about AI usage. According to Pew Research, 2021 saw 31% of people ages 18-29 say they were “more concerned than excited” about AI. However, that number skyrocketed to 55% in 2026. Young adults have also expressed more concern about AI taking their jobs. It should come as no surprise that most college students are going to be against the usage of AI slop as a result, and we don’t want to see it anywhere. There are discussions that are worth having over why people use AI for graphics. Some organizations do not have dedicated graphic designers or they can’t afford to pay an artist. But for a university, there is no excuse. The university has a bachelor of fine arts in graphic and digital design. There are plenty of opportunities for students to get involved in designing for many organizations and accounts on campus. The university’s Art + Design page showcases the work that these students do, and not giving these artists chances is a missed opportunity. In addition, many non-graphic design students outside of their studies do art as a hobby or side job. Students will do anything to boost their resume – even if they do things for free. When I see flyers around campus or stories on Instagram from clubs or groups that are AI-generated, am I supposed to take them seriously? When I see the university’s theater program posting AI flyers for their auditions and productions, would I even want to go see either of them? When I see Sigma Alpha Epsilon posting AI for public relations and their “Rush Week” schedule, would I want to be recruited or take part in any of these events, or go elsewhere? Then, when the Military Veterans at the University of New Haven page posts AI slop, is there any respect towards those who served our country? On Sept. 12, the university posted a carousel of pictures to their Instagram and Facebook pages of jewels attached to campus landmarks. The comments section was filled with angry messages that called out the AI slop, complained about “cutting corners,” tuition being high and some even said they were glad they dropped out or transferred from the school. When something like this happens among the student body, trust issues can develop. How do you expect students to trust you after posting something that comes from AI data centers that 70% of Americans oppose. Additionally, when people say they oppose these data centers, why go and post AI slop? It is extremely hypocritical and only enables more data centers to be built when you’re complicit, especially when people use AI slop to post anti-data center propaganda. This is something where you can’t fight fire with fire. In response to the comments, the university’s Instagram account said, “We hear you. This was intended to be a creative take on the bedazzled social media trend, blending traditional design techniques with generative AI. We appreciate the feedback and remain committed to showcasing the talents, creativity, and experiences of our students across our channels.” Keeping the post up is also a public relations nightmare. You continue to run the risk of students continuing to make negative comments. It almost feels like they want the post to stay up and endorse the usage of AI for content. To improve transparency and stand against AI art for the future, I have a few recommendations. A big step would be for the Undergraduate Student Government Association to ban Resident Student Organizations from using AI to make their flyers and posts. The university could also establish a pool for students who can make flyers for organizations and social media. To students, the use of AI graphics is an insult. Let’s make these wrongs right and throw AI slop in the trash where it belongs. The Student News Source of the University of New Haven Your email address will not be published. title: How to Turn Your Marketing Internship into a Full-Time Job - unh.edu
content: Paige Spencer ’26, center, with Office Interiors Limited President Ellen Bates, left, and Director of Design Erin King at the company’s Dover, New Hampshire, office. Heading into her final semester, marketing student Paige Spencer '26 was looking for an internship where she could gain real-world experience while completing her senior capstone project, which challenges students to help a business improve its marketing efforts. At the same time, Ellen Bates, president of Dover-based Office Interiors Limited, attended a UNH CEO & Family Enterprise Center meeting where Cayce Jones, director of UNH Paul College Career and Professional Success, spoke about the value interns can bring to small businesses. Bates decided it was time to act. Her women-led commercial interior design and furniture firm needed someone who could "change its marketing game." Office Interiors then posted the internship on employment website Handshake seeking its own version of Emily in Paris—the Netflix series about a young marketing professional documenting her experiences on social media. What followed was a perfect match. Spencer turned the internship into a full-time marketing coordinator position while helping the 40-year-old company modernize its digital presence. Rather than applying through the posting, Spencer reached out directly to Bates with her qualifications and a creative video introducing herself. "She showed initiative by figuring out who I was and emailing me directly. On top of that, she created a video of herself from locations around the world, including the Eiffel Tower. We had specifically encouraged applicants to stand out in the posting — to be creative and show us who they were — and Paige did that in full force,” Bates says. Spencer didn't want to be just another applicant. Instead, she focused on getting in front of the people making the hiring decision. “As soon as I saw the opportunity, I thought, 'This seems like a great company, I need to meet them,'" Spencer says. Office Interiors had an inconsistent social media presence and a website that didn't fully showcase its work. Spencer tackled both. “When I started, there was an opportunity to modernize the company’s digital presence and better showcase its work,” Spencer says. “We refreshed social media, focused on growing our audience, and from there, my role expanded into broader marketing and brand strategy.” One of Spencer's proudest achievements was rebuilding the company's website from scratch—even though she had never designed one before. She taught herself the process through online tutorials and experimentation, then focused on creating a more visual website that used photos and video to better showcase Office Interiors' work. "The website was a big win. We're always busy doing great work, and we have so much talent and so many projects to showcase,” says Erin King, director of design at Office Interiors. “Paige took that content and turned it into something worthy of a website. We worked together to gather the photos, and she pulled it all together. I think it's one of our best tools because people don't cold call anymore. The website is our face — it's our cold call." Bates and King say Spencer struck a balance between collaboration and initiative. She wasn't afraid to ask questions, but she was equally comfortable taking ownership of new projects. "It became obvious during her internship that when she graduated, we had to keep her. There was no question about it," Bates says. Building the company's new website was only the beginning. In her full-time role, Spencer continued expanding Office Interiors' marketing efforts by developing a social media strategy centered on three content pillars: educating customers about the design process, showcasing completed projects,  and giving followers a behind-the-scenes look at the company's culture. Her role also grew beyond digital marketing. She began tracking marketing analytics, representing Office Interiors at networking events, and helping plan company initiatives, including its upcoming 40th anniversary celebration and fundraiser. "I liked social media and content marketing. Now that I'm doing it, I kind of love all parts of marketing," Spencer says. "We wear a lot of different hats. But I love it. No day is the same." Bates says Spencer's willingness to keep learning has benefited both her career and the company. The new website and her broader marketing efforts have already generated new business and helped raise Office Interiors' profile. "Paige is becoming the face of Office Interiors when it comes to marketing," Bates says. "She's representing us at networking events and with the organizations we're involved in, in addition to everything she does in the office. We're asking a lot of her." Looking back, Spencer says her biggest piece of advice is to treat the internship search like the first step in your career “Research the company first and make sure it’s a place where you can see yourself growing,” Spencer says. “Then go all in. Find ways to stand out, take initiative, and look for problems you can help solve. Don’t just treat an internship like something to put on your résumé, treat it like the first step in your career.” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.

EHTH recently said small and mid-sized employers are facing a sharp jump in health insurance costs for 2027, pushing many to rethink traditional group coverage. Its survey of more than 500 business owners and managers found that 54% expect premium increases of at least 10%, while more than one in five face hikes of 15% or higher. Last month, Aon plc AON projected that U.S. employer healthcare costs will rise 9.5% in 2027 before employers take steps to rein in expenses. Aon links the increase not only to higher prices but also to greater healthcare utilization and a more expensive mix of services. Marsh & McLennan Companies, Inc. MRSH expects an even steeper 11% increase before cost-control measures, moderating to 8.2% after employers make planned benefit changes. That would mark the sharpest increase in employer health benefit costs since 2003, even after cost-containment efforts. Marsh also found that 59% of employers plan benefit changes, including higher deductibles, as companies try to contain spending. It attributes the expected increase to several factors, including costly new therapies, higher provider rates, broader use of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, AI-supported medical billing and out-of-network charges. GLP-1 drugs alone are projected to contribute roughly one percentage point to health benefit cost growth in 2027. eHealth CEO Derrick Duke said that rising costs are making it harder for employers to use health benefits to attract and retain workers. The company sees growing interest in alternatives such as Custom Health Option and Individual Care Expense (CHOICE) Arrangements, also known as Individual Coverage Health Reimbursement Arrangements (ICHRAs), which can offer employers more cost certainty, flexibility and simpler administration. The numbers suggest that higher premiums are starting to change how smaller employers think about providing health benefits. Among companies facing rate increases, 80% said the size of the hike surprised them. The bigger concern is that 73% are considering moving away from traditional group coverage in 2027. Another 85% worry they may be unable to afford group coverage within three years. Meanwhile, 58% are already pursuing alternatives, while awareness of CHOICE Arrangements rose to 57% from 46% a year earlier, a meaningful eleven-point increase. For eHealth, this trend could expand the market for employer-funded individual coverage. If more small and mid-sized companies move away from fully insured group plans, demand could rise for CHOICE Arrangements and other options that eHealth can help employers and workers evaluate. Several studies have shown limited to no success of brokerage recommendations in guiding investors to pick stocks with the best price increase potential. Are you wondering why?
